Goodwill Industries of South Central California has announced their intentions to open a new 7,000 square-foot secondhand retail location in The Orchard Shopping Center, located at 655 Tucker Road Suite B.
The site was the former home to Family Dollar prior to their merger with Dollar Tree and consolidation of several sites, including the store in Tehachapi.

The store will serve as both a retail store and donation center for local families, Goodwill representatives say the new location will also create 17 new jobs in the City of Tehachapi, part of Goodwill’s mission of strengthening the local economy while helping individuals gain valuable skills and work experience.
It is anticipated that customers can expect nearly 20,000 pieces of clothing and 10,000 housewares available on the sales floor with over 1,500 items added daily.
The Tehachapi location will sell both merchandise donated locally and donated items from other Goodwill donation centers around Kern County.
The second-hand market continues to be one of the fastest growing retail sectors in the United States boasting 14% growth in 2024, which was the strongest annual gain since 2021.
Secondhand retail is also outpacing the broader retail clothing market by five times according to a Global Data study conducted in March of 2025.
The same report claims that of those surveyed, 59% of consumers say that if government policies and tariffs make apparel more expensive, they will seek more affordable secondhand options.

In addition, respondents claim they plan to spend 34% of their apparel budget on secondhand items in the next 12 months with younger generations such as Gen Z and Millennials claiming they plan to spend 46% on secondhand clothing.

Goodwill’s presence in the City of Tehachapi becomes the third secondhand store joining the Tehachapi Hospital Guild and Sharing & Caring, also non-profit entities who donate proceeds to other charitable causes.

Placer.ai data suggests that the presence of Goodwill will not reduce the number of shoppers at current secondhand stores, in the last 12 months the Hospital Guild has had 40,000 visitors while Sharing and Caring had 21,000.

Both locations had an average “visit frequency” of 2.8, meaning each customer accounted for visited each location nearly three times, suggesting that secondhand shopping drives repeat visitors to multiple locations.

Additionally, both the Hospital Guild and Sharing and Caring are often limited in the quantity of donated items they can accept, leading to those items either being throw away, or, being donated at other secondhand stores outside of Tehachapi, where they are sold without any local benefit.
The City of Tehachapi has been on Goodwill’s radar for several years, with the location and demographics of the market being an attractive asset for the organization.
First, Tehachapi’s income level suggests that donations will be more frequent with higher quality items being donated.
Of the combined 60,000 visitors to both the Hospital Guild and Sharing and Caring, nearly 40% of customers were from households with an income between $100,000 and $200,000 according to Placer.ai.
Goodwill representatives released the following statement regarding their hopes for the Tehachapi market and their impact on the community.
Work will begin shortly on the staffing for this location, the interior setup and stocking as well as exterior signage in anticipation of their grand opening yet to be determined.
The Tehachapi store will be the 11 th location under for Goodwill Industries of South Central California joining sites in Bakersfield, Delano, Porterville, Hanford and Taft.
For more information visit www.thegoodwill.org.
ICSC marked another successful venture into the retail world for the City of Tehachapi connecting with brokers, owners and site selectors for new businesses within our City.
The focus this year was to assist with retail vacancies left throughout various shopping centers and working with brokers as businesses shuffle around the City as they grow and expand.

In addition, economic factors with private businesses are leading to closures nationally, so positioning those properties for the next tenants as soon as possible was also at the forefront and showed considerable promise.

While many of the “deals” so to speak are still outstanding until formal permits are applied for with the City, there will be several new businesses making their presence felt in Tehachapi as they repurpose existing retail space for a new business opportunity, some of which are filling retail leakage gaps and will allow for more spending to be kept local and not sent to other markets outside of the City of Tehachapi.
Both national brands and local small businesses are benefiting from this shift and occupancy of existing retail space.
As pointed out earlier, the Tehachapi Towne Center, the City’s oldest shopping center, went from nearly 50% vacant 18 months ago to over 85% occupied with the addition of new businesses.

The Tehachapi Rite Aid, one of the original tenants, will be closing due to their corporate bankruptcy filing, however, that site is not expected to be vacant long as interest and conversations with another national retailer have already taken place and will continue to do so once lease terms are available for negotiation following the closure of the Rite Aid location.
ICSC represents long-term investment in relationships with site selectors, brokers and owners that can materialize in a business presence in the City of Tehachapi.
This process can range from 12 to 36 months depending on a variety of external factors including economic conditions, labor costs, franchisee location and more.
Some of the most recent brands that located to Tehachapi following years of ICSC interaction including Anytime Fitness, Jersey Mike’s Subs, Chipotle, and Panda Express.
Other brands that have been established longer within this market but were also built on ICSC relationships include The Home Depot, Walmart and Tractor Supply.

The City of Tehachapi will continue to participate in both ICSC and ICSC Western, which is a smaller event in the fall that focuses solely on brands that are actively expanding within the California market.

The Tehachapi Town Center, the first traditional shopping center to open in the City of Tehachapi in the early 1990’s, still features a few original anchor tenants, including Save Mart Supermarket, Jack-In-The Box, plus Rite-Aid (initially Thrifty Drug Store prior to Rite Aid’s acquisition of the brand), but several other tenants have come and gone in the 30-plus years of the center’s existence.

Recently however, thanks in part to renovations to the center, and a changing demand for local services, several of the available store fronts are occupied, or in the tenant improvement phase for a new business openings in the near future.

First, there was TehachaSleep, the local mattress and furniture store that relocated from Downtown Tehachapi to suite 831, where more than 4,000 s.f. of space was available for displays, storage and customer service.
The same owners of TehachaSleep also operate Tehachapi Christian Store, which will also be relocating to suite 821A in Tehachapi Town Center from their Downtown location.

In addition, following the corporate closure of all Sears Hometown Stores, including the Tehachapi franchise, Anytime Fitness took over suite 835A for their new state-of-the-art fitness center opening in May.

A pair of local business owners are also expanding their offerings by applying to convert suite 821E into a party supply store, with the national closures of places such as Party City, the opportunity to scale a business like that into a local offering has potential.

The former Tea Donuts, at 807B has been purchased as is undergoing tenant improvements as well to open under new ownership as “T Donuts.” These recent new businesses have transformed the center from seven vacancies at this time a year ago to just three, including the large 3,600 s.f. office building formerly occupied by the Tehachapi Area Association of Realtors.
The center is now 85% occupied with new foot traffic expected with the Anytime Fitness opening, which retail trends suggest drive traffic to surrounding businesses and services.
The City of Tehachapi has collaborated closely with tenants and the brokers at Cushman & Wakefield to tell our story and encourage investment in this center, along with other vacancies in the city.
Every building goes through a development cycle that includes new construction, improvements and a shift in tenants.
This power corner featuring the oldest shopping center in the City of Tehachapi is a true success story and will see a great transformation as 2025 continues.

There is a continued push within the City to collaborate with owners and brokers to fill vacancies within the Starbucks center in Capital Hills, and Tehachapi Crossing, where the former Big Papa’s Restaurant closed in late 2023.

With growth in the nearby renewable energy, mining and aerospace sectors, Tehachapi continues to be a destination sought after by highly educated and well-paid employees.

Each project has some ties to Tehachapi and is expected to bring additional economic impact during both construction and operations.

The California Supreme Court ruled last week in a rare pre-election review, that the proposed “Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act,” was unconstitutional in the State of California and instructed the secretary of state to not place the measure on the November 2024 statewide general election ballot.

The initiative was funded by the California Business Roundtable, an organization comprised of some of California’s wealthiest corporations, who were seeking to revise the California Constitution to reclassify many fees in State and local governments as “taxes” which would then require a two-thirds votes of the electorate to be implemented.
It also sought to undo several voter-approved tax measures over the last several years if they did not include a specific sunset clause.
The measure would have redefined what was considered a fee or a tax in the Constitution, an act that the legislature argued was not available via initiative.

In their opinion, the Supreme Court ruled that while amendments to the State Constitution are allowable via voter referendum, revisions to the constitution are not, and require either a two-thirds vote of the legislature to be placed on the ballot or a state constitutional convention.
The measure would have challenged millions of impact fees, code enforcement penalties and put at risk hundreds of approved voter referendums passed prior to the enacting of this initiative.

Currently, local governments are allowed to study and charge impact fees to developers for the impacts their projects have on utilities and traffic, this initiative would have opened thousands of legal challenges to those fees and require an even broader nexus between the fees charged and the projects they would benefit.

Locally, this initiative would not have only challenged fees in the City of Tehachapi but put into question the November 2022 local voter approval of Measure S, the cities essential services and local control measure, since the sunset on that measure was “until ended by voters” and not a hard date sunset.

While the City of Tehachapi was vocal in their opposition, as witnessed by the resolution to oppose the measure passed by the City Council in 2023, supporters of the Business Roundtable initiative claimed in written correspondence that Measure S “should” be safe, since it did include some sort of a sunset clause. “Should” however is shaky legal ground that could have opened the measure, which was passed by nearly 60% of voters in the city, to costly legal challenges.
Locally, impact fees are charged to developers to pay for their long-term impact to a system, such as wastewater.
Those funds are placed in an account and when the need arises to expand such infrastructure, that money is utilized.

If the fees were significantly lower, as desired by the referendum’s backers, current ratepayers, business owners and residents would bear the cost of improvement in their rates, a bad business practice that benefits development at the cost of current residents.
In their decision, the California Supreme Court pointed to something as simple as a usage fee for a recreation department.
If a department wished to increase the usage fee of a recreation center to pay for operating expenses, that fee would be subject to a ballot vote.
Currently the State Legislature and the California Constitution allows local jurisdictions to increase such fees in a reasonable manner to cover the costs of delivering services.

The Tehachapi City Council joined hundreds of Cities across California to advocate against this measure via the League of California Cities, as it had the potential to strip away local control for the benefit of large corporations.
League of California Cities CEO Carolyn Coleman released this statement after the court’s decision.

From an economic development perspective, this ruling allows the City of Tehachapi to not only continue delivering and budgeting for the vital infrastructure and public safety services promised in the approval of Measure S in 2022, but also continue to study and charge reasonable development impact fees for water, wastewater, parks & recreation, traffic and administration, to ensure new development is not subsidized by the city’s general fund.

Fees are updated regularly and required to be studied every five years prior to any increases with a certified engineer’s report including an analysis of a reasonable cost estimate of future infrastructure expansions.

The City of Tehachapi recently attended the Innovating Commerce, Serving Communities (ICSC) annual conference in Las Vegas, which is the largest gathering of retail brokers, site selectors, franchises, development and retail firms in the world.

This annual event is an opportunity for the City of Tehachapi to showcase our market, retail vacancies and assist brokers in addressing the needs of our community in relation to the ever-evolving retail world.

The City of Tehachapi’s approach has shifted over the years from a blanketing approach to a more targeted effort that relies on personal relationships with retail brokers and representatives of properties.

Since brokers deal with franchises large and small across various communities, their relationships are valuable in not only filling vacancies, but also convincing brands and franchises to discover the Tehachapi market and vast trade area supported by City businesses.

For example, meetings with one broker over the course of the last few years, both at ICSC and via multiple conversations have led to the signing of leases and letters of intent for two national brands that will be coming to the City of Tehachapi once their formal applications are submitted.
Both of which will occupy high-traffic retail areas while filling voids in the community.

In addition, meetings and brainstorming with other brokerages, recently retained by local property owners to assist with their properties were also productive and are expected to lead to new tenants within the next 12 months.

As the brokers navigate the commercial real estate world and focus on lease terms and language, the City of Tehachapi assists by sharing information, telling our story, touting the benefits of our market with real data and showing the potential earnings for the right business in the right location.

With the changing retail world challenges still exist in filling some vacancies, especially those in the “big box” format where costs to renovate large spaces into smaller retail offerings remain high, leaving many tenants interested, but worried about capital expenses and the amount of time needed to see a return on investment.
However, smaller suites and storefronts remain attractive, even in older developments as the small format store makes more economic sense for investors currently.

Over the last decade, relationships built at ICSC events have resulted in millions of dollars of local retail, hospitality and restaurant investments including Walmart, Home Depot, Big 5, Tractor Supply, Panda Express, and Chipotle just to name a few.

These investments assist in reducing retail leakage (money spent outside of Tehachapi) increase local revenue which results in the delivery of better City services including public safety, road maintenance and quality of life initiatives.

In addition, economic impact which calculates how locally spent dollars result in more local spending from employees to small businesses, local vendors, restaurants and service providers is also increased.

The City of Tehachapi regularly participates in both the national ICSC convention in Las Vegas and follows up with visits and meetings at the ICSC Western show each fall which is a more targeted western United States focus for retailers, restaurants and site selectors.
California Growers are Removing Vines, Why is Tehachapi trending in the opposite direction?

A new report from the San Francisco Chronicle claims that California’s wine grapes are too readily available, forcing many vineyard owners to pull up their crops as the market is saturated with more California wine grapes than ever before.

This oversupply, coupled with an influx of cheaper grapes from places like Argentina and Chile, used oftentimes to blend with California grapes while keeping them California wines, is leading many growers to abandon their crops altogether.

The Chronicle claims that there are too many wine grapes planted in California for the market to sustain, this has been the case recently when family vineyards up and down the state have had difficulty selling wine grapes to larger wine makers, due in part to both cheaper international alternatives and reports that California, and the nation, are drinking less wine.
What does this approach mean for the ‘Tehachapi Mountains’ wine producers?
Tehachapi is one of the newer American Viticultural Areas in the state and is currently operating six wineries and tasting rooms in both the City of Tehachapi and the Cummings Valley Area.
These wineries attract tourists, locals, special events, live music and of course, local wines from grapes mostly grown on site.
So, is the California wine grape market and the consumption of less wine impacting Tehachapi’s relatively new wine region?
For that, we check the numbers from five of our local tasting rooms using Placer.ai location-based data available from the City of Tehachapi.

Those numbers indicate that not only did Tehachapi see a new tasting room open in 2023 (Stray Leaves in Downtown), but compared to 2022, the visitation numbers from these tasting rooms in total remained unchanged in 2023.

In 2022, Tehachapi tasting rooms saw 59,500 visitors, in 2023, that number was 59,400, a relative statistical wash to the previous year. 2023 numbers account for the opening of Stray Leaves downtown, a long-awaited tasting room, the first to be located in the incorporated city limits.
They are not the only ones still looking to get a piece of the “Tehachapi Mountains” AVA.
The Kern County Planning Commission has received an application for a new winery and tasting room to be located adjacent to Tehachapi Wine and Cattle in Cummings Valley.
The City of Tehachapi has sent a letter of support for the applicant and the project as agricultural tourism is itself a valuable commodity.

While Tehachapi’s visitation is down somewhat compared to the “Covid Years” of 2020 and much of 2021, when the Tehachapi climate attracted many visitors due to the ability to sit outside and enjoy wine without the heat of other wine regions or burdensome regulations, the trend remains consistent in normal years with more players and investment into the region.
The difference?
Most of the Tehachapi wine grape growers use their grapes for their own products, sometimes blending with others and sometimes selling what they themselves cannot bottle.

In addition, the Tehachapi Mountain grapes are a heartier fruit with thicker wine skins, additional sweetness and flavor thanks to the cooler overnight temperatures compared to their heat-soaked valley counterparts.
The fruit is simply grown at a higher elevation than most, leading it to be a special product used in specialty wines compared to valley-grown crops.

Tehachapi’s wine industry continues to attract visitors, many day trippers from nearby communities, as well as those visiting, the presence of the industry has led to an estimated 1200 hotel stays over the last year, which includes special events such as weddings and parties hosted by many of the tasting rooms.

While California’s wine industry might be over growing their crops, the uniqueness of Tehachapi’s high altitude wine region continues to support the local industry and create an attractive opportunity for expansion due to a unique product and local experience.
The economic development goals in the City of Tehachapi heavily rely on the ability of a local police department and emergency dispatch center to protect the investments of local businesses.
As other cities in California cut police spending, resulting in rising crime and organized retail theft leading to business closures, the City of Tehachapi has taken a much different approach.
Leveraging the work of the police department to not only protect businesses, but build cases against organized thieves, oftentimes working with neighboring jurisdictions to bring them to justice.

In the last month, the Tehachapi Police Department has led two investigations, partnering with the Bakersfield Police Department to recover assets and merchandise stolen from Tehachapi and moved to other areas in Kern County.
Here are two news articles relating to those cases and the lengths that TPD will go to in order to protect local businesses.
Understanding that many of these crimes are committed by those living outside the area, the ability to build investigations with the assistance of other local authorities is paramount.
In order for those type of cases to continue, investing in the police department locally is a benefit to the community and business owners.

Here are a few snap shots from our FY 2023-24 budget, as you can see, the Tehachapi Police Department is the highest general fund expense within City departments, with continued investments in the department, which also features its own dispatch center, so calls to 9-1-1 are answered locally making the response times quicker than those of surrounding agencies who rely on either the Sheriff’s Department dispatch center in Bakersfield, or the California Highway Patrol dispatch center in Bishop, CA.

Our economic development goals heavily involve the police department as we tout our ability to “protect your investment” the City of Tehachapi cannot attract new businesses without the police delivering on that priority, and they certainly do.
We are also very community-facing with the police department under our new Chief of Police Richard Standridge who started in Tehachapi in July of 2023.

As a result, TPD have initiated several community programs that are leading to the formation of a Police Activities League leveraging some new Pickleball courts and Five-A-Side soccer park we are building in the community.

The message for businesses looking to expand is to not give up on California due to certain cities’ politics and that there is a place remaining that is going to protect investments and provide safety to staff and customers.

With the close of the calendar just around the corner the City of Tehachapi continues to assess Economic Development priorities, recruitment, retention and reuse efforts within our City.

As has been tradition in recent years, an annual S.W.O.T. analysis is conducted and was recently presented as part of the Greater Tehachapi Economic Development Council meeting which investigates the Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats as we head into 2024 in economic development.

This internal assessment assists in ensuring that strengths are being properly leveraged, weaknesses are either addressed, or at least realized in certain aspects when it comes to business development, opportunities are sought after and planned for while threats are realized, and property addressed in all efforts.
As some say, when it comes to real estate and throwing a fastball it is all about location, location, location.
As seen in the graphic, the City of Tehachapi had 1.2 million people make a total of 7.3 million visits to the city limits in 2023.

This number assists greatly in marketing a city of 10,000 residents and the impact it has from the retail and business perspective, not only to the additional 30,000 residents in the unincorporated Tehachapi communities, but also the traveling public along Highway 58 and those utilizing our businesses from surrounding Kern County communities and cities.
The cost of living in the City of Tehachapi is not “low” but it is “lower” thank much of the State and in many cases the U.S. average.
As seen above, BestPlaces.net scores the City of Tehachapi just below the national average for the cost of total living, and 33% lower than the average for the State of California.
This is a selling point for businesses in and around the city who need reasonably priced housing a living expenses for employees.
Home prices in the City of Tehachapi spiked in 2022 but have seen a reasonable leveling out in 2023 as newer inventory comes on the market.
The average selling price for a single-family home in 2023 was $390,900, which is above the National average but nearly 48% lower than the average selling price in the State of California.

The City of Tehachapi is blessed to be the benefactor of so many community organizations, non-profit entities and volunteers that not only shape this community but support and organize special events that drive local and tourism traffic into our City.

The City of Tehachapi has taken a more proactive role in either hosting events (Farmer’s Market, July 4 th Festival, Hometown Christmas) while also supplying support for other events (Mountain Festival, Apple Festival, Memorial Day, etc.).

By ensuring these events run smoothly, the attendee experience is a positive one which increases the likelihood of not only returning to that event in the future but also spending more time exploring or returning to our community.
Here is a data report of the 2023 Apple Festival showing not only 10,000 visitors but also some of the most popular before and after destinations in the City during that event.
Daytime population.
Many retailers bank their business model on the “daytime population” those that work in a community and are more likely to spend money either at a restaurant or retailer during their lunch hour.

For Tehachapi, we have many residents that commute to our surrounding industries outside of Tehachapi, while we import many workers for retail and other businesses, the daytime population remains lower than many businesses would like to see.

The graphic below represents the entire Tehachapi area labor force, however with the City of Tehachapi being the sought-after business location for many sectors as explained in many strengths above, the entire area’s workforce impacts potential business recruitment.
While there is no long-term solution to this issue, attracting businesses desiring to both be located and employ local continues to be one small avenue for chipping away at this number.

It is no secret that while the City of Tehachapi is a more affordable lifestyle than most of the State of California, certain state regulations as it relates to employment law, benefits and regulations make operating in the State more expensive than the National average.
This risk is realized by businesses both seeking to expand or to invest in our City.
However, it can be a weakness when State mandated costs often surpass many of the other costs that impact the bottom line of a business.
In addition, building regulations above and beyond those centered around safety add additional costs to new development within any community in the State.

This is both a strength and an opportunity, the fact that the City of Tehachapi plays an integral supporting role near so many existing and emerging industries including renewable energy, mining, construction, law enforcement, defense, space exploration and more.

These high-paying careers attract a workforce that are looking for a family-friendly community to call home and oftentimes that cannot be found in larger cities in the Antelope or San Joaquin Valleys.
These jobs however do not just mean one job, it means several jobs created by the existence of one job within a certain sector.
The chart below shows the multiplier effect for one job in each of the sectors, many of which we have in abundance in and around the City of Tehachapi.
Those industries create additional job opportunities into a local economy.
For example, as seen below, one new construction job creates an additional four jobs within their local economy.
Businesses close for a variety of reasons, some internal, some external and some economical.
While many might see retail vacancies as a “Weakness,” it is a marketable opportunity.
With the costs of new construction, sometimes it is more convenient for a business to renovate an available space to meet their needs as opposed from building from the ground up.
The City of Tehachapi has several prime retail and restaurant availabilities that provide an excellent starting point for a new business.
While closing any business is a loss for a community, it is also an opportunity for someone else to come in and repurpose that space and bring a new perspective or business model to the property.

In addition, the City of Tehachapi has cultivated relationships with commercial real estate brokers, most of which are located outside of Tehachapi, to discuss lease rates, terms and assist in seeking potential local or regional businesses to occupy those spaces.
These relationships are critical for outside brokers to understand the City of Tehachapi market and economic situation.
There are many existential threats that are consistently being addressed within business operations in the City of Tehachapi.

Many of those are centered around new California laws or proposed initiatives from the State Legislature, many of which make sense for larger cities, but have an unreasonable impact on small cities like Tehachapi.

For example, recently signed legislation to mandate minimum wage increases for fast food workers will lead to some pay increases, but also potentially create a labor vacuum in the food service industry as many “back of the house” staff at a full-service restaurant, will elect to take a higher wage at a fast-food establishment, creating work shortages within the full-service restaurant industry.

Since California legislation tends to draw attention from other states who occasionally emulate them, the fast-food industry has already started testing artificial intelligence and other automated technologies within their organization which will eliminate some of the jobs to minimize the costs of goods to the consumer.
However, some of those costs, both in the food service industry and the health care industry, who have also had legislation passed mandating pay increases, will be felt by consumers and rate payers.

An initiative, proposed by some of California’s wealthiest corporations, entitled the ‘Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act’ slated for a November 2024 vote, has been opposed by the Tehachapi City Council along with several other members of the League of California Cities.
This measure, while attractive to many in title, passes many of the developer impact fees on to current rate payers and residents while reducing the costs of development.

This measure also threatens the City of Tehachapi’s recently approved Measure S that increased the sales tax rate in the city to 8.25% since the sunset clause of “until ended by voters” is not a specific date.
The constitutionality of this measure has been challenged in the California Supreme Court, with arguments due in February.

This initiative would harm local revenues by redefining many legally adopted fees for development and fines for code enforcement violations as “taxes” and changing many other areas of the California Constitution that redefine the criteria for charging impact and utility connection fees.

Other California polices and budget priorities, especially those related to the Corrections industry have already impacted Tehachapi with a pair of facilities closed over the last two years at California Correctional Facility in Tehachapi.

While most of the jobs associated with those closures have been protected or transferred to nearby institutions keeping those families within the Tehachapi economy, the incarcerated count at CCI has been drastically reduced, leaving eyes on the next budget cycle regarding any future closures.

Historically since the expansion of CCI in the 1980’s, corrections have been an important employment sector in the community, while any additional cuts could harm the local economy, it would not have the drastic impact due to the diversity of employment sectors now in and around the City of Tehachapi.
This S.W.O.T. analysis will be used to ensure that strengths and opportunities are being leveraged while weaknesses and threats are properly addressed.
It also serves as a roadmap for priorities for the City of Tehachapi economic development as goals and objectives are created as part of the 2024-25 fiscal budget year.

“Smart City” is a buzz term associated with a city’s desire to transition operations and actions in both the public and private sector into more tangible and efficient results with a targeted outcome in mind.

Many years ago, the term was associated simply with connectivity, which mostly meant a quality fiber-optic internet connection for residents and businesses, along with public Wi-Fi to encourage connectivity and business operations.

While those elements remain, recent technological advancements in artificial intelligence, labor, automation and work performance have opened the door for the City of Tehachapi to start looking towards the applicability of those advances in our own operations.

Additionally, those same advancements are not limited to government operations, and offer the private sector and many partners the same ability to make data-driven decisions for a more efficient and productive outcome.

The City of Tehachapi is leading the way in using data-driven decisions in many areas of our operations, an effort that began with Economic Development a few years ago with the addition of Placer.ai location-based data to assist in the recruitment of new and retention of existing businesses.

As the platform as grown, that technology not only assists in understanding the trade area demographics of the City, but also assists with decisions regarding traffic, development site plans and travel patterns to plan for safer projects.

New technologies in other City departments are also being tested to assist in delivering better services to residents and customers while compiling useful information to help in operations and better-addressing issues before they become larger problems for our residents.
In the private sector, new technology, especially that in the food service industry, are offering the potential for more efficient business operations.

With the rising costs of labor in the State of California, including the recently signed bill by Governor Gavin Newsom that required a $20 an hour minimum wage for fast-food workers, competition for food service labor will increase.
Couple that with the necessity to pass rising staff costs on to customers and many corporate entities are exploring additional options that could soon be present in Tehachapi.
Recently, Chipotle announced their testing of an automated process to build all salad and bowl orders.
One of their automated bots is already in place, known as “Chippy” that produces the chain’s tortilla chips.

Burger King has unveiled a new store design and concept that will among other things, increase the efficiency of their drive thrus while also adding additional kiosks for ordering inside their stores, technology that they had previously been slow to adopt.

While they do not have a location in Tehachapi, the White Castle chain recently signed an agreement with Samsung and SoundHound to provide voice-enabled AI enabled dynamic menu boards using SoundHound’s proprietary voice-recognition technology.
Should these dynamic menu boards work, it is very likely they will be adopted by every major fast food chain since the drive thru generates the majority of quick service restaurant business.
Self-checkout technology, nothing new but recently improved with additional monitoring and capabilities, has become commonplace in grocery stores but is also expanding to other businesses.

Recently Tehachapi’s Flying J Travel Center replaced registers with self-checkout kiosks that are only assisted by an employee, allowing for quicker check outs and an allocation of labor resources to other areas of the vast travel center that has served over 600,000 customers in the last 12 months.

Smaller automations and technology are more prevalent now than ever in small establishments as many local restaurants utilize mobile card readers for diner checkout or print customer specific QR codes on table checks to allow customers to scan and pay via apps such as Toast.

The “smart tickets” so to speak, allow for systems to capture what items were sold, this data can later be used to assist a small business owner in better understanding inventory and the performance of certain menu items, a valuable tool in times of higher food costs.
These types of technologies and data-driven decisions are applicable among almost all business sectors and will advance as all cities continue to grow smarter.
Whether it be AI or other automation, finding ways to increase efficiency is crucial for all businesses, including small business owners who traditionally have tight profit margins.

Similarly, as our private sector partners continue to embrace advances that work for them, the City of Tehachapi will do the same, seeking ways to become a Smart(er) city in the future with hopes to formalize that vision in the very near future with community stakeholder and partner input.

The Tehachapi City Council unanimously approved the creation of the ‘Economic Development Support Fund’ and its first grant opportunity, the city’s ‘Small Business Sign Grant Program,’ on September 18 th.

The sign grant program is available to small businesses in the City of Tehachapi and works as a reimbursement fund where accepted applicants can have a portion of their sign purchase costs reimbursed with the City minimum of $500 and a maximum of $3,000.
The entire list of rules and regulations can be found on the Sign Grant Improvement Program website.

The purpose of the program is to continue to unique look and feel of Tehachapi commercial signs while assisting small business owners with one of their most costly items when opening or maintaining their business.
Each sign must adhere to the City of Tehachapi sign standards and go through the staff and planning commission approvals as applicable.
The details of sign standards are also available on the website, but staff is available to answer questions and review proposed designs from applicants.
To assist with this, the application process includes one-on-one meetings with applicants to verify eligibility, discuss designs, potential costs and the sign approval process.
The ‘Economic Development Support Fund’ has been allocated $30,000 for this initial Small Business Sign Grant Program.
This funding was made available via ‘Measure S’ funds, the additional one-cent sales tax initiative approved by voters in November of 2022.
As part of the outreach process, residents identified “protecting local businesses and jobs” as one of the funding priorities for the additional revenue.
The goal of this program is to assist small businesses with sign costs so their capital can be used elsewhere in the startup or operation of their small business.
For more information about the Sign Improvement Grant Program please visit our website for details and the application process.

One of the most valuable tools in economic development, and one of the most important skills, is matching business with potential customers.
Business owners, developers and site selectors want to match their business with the customers that already exist in a city or a trade area while also considering the potential market to be captured.
There is a reason and a rationale behind every development and site placement decision.
Pick the right site matched with the right demographic customer profile that matches a business and you will be successful.
Guess at the results or anticipate some major change without proper research and potentially set a business up for failure.

In a secondary market like the City of Tehachapi, understanding the consumers in the City, surrounding unincorporated Tehachapi and other nearby communities (included in the City’s trade area), is paramount to assisting both large and small businesses into our area and providing the best opportunity for success.
That being said, who are we?
Recent Census data and other data sets are painting a more complete picture about the City of Tehachapi and the City’s trade area in recent years thanks to evolving technology.

Here’s a brief recap of who we are according to STI:Popstats, an accurate quarterly population and demographics dataset used in conjunction with the City of Tehachapi’s Placer.ai location-based data services.

In the City of Tehachapi Trade Area, the **Median Household Income** is $82,000, which is above the national average. **The average household income** is just over $106,000. **Disposable income per household** is just over $70,000, putting it above the national average.
With those numbers also comes the 10% of the trade area considered to be below the poverty line.
So, there is a variety in both income, disposable income and poverty levels within the customers in the City of Tehachapi trade area.

Creating the household income are job types, the trade area **consists of the top industries** as 17% in education, an additional 16.5% in the construction/mining industries, 15% in retail and 13% in public administration.

27 percent of households have children while the **average household size** is 2.63 (lets round up to three so we can count the full person). **Ethnicity** is broken down as follows: White (70%), Hispanic (21%), African American (3%), Asian (1%), Other (5%).
**Education levels** have increased significantly over the years with the addition of more skilled labor associated with employment sectors located around the Tehachapi area.
Past High School, 30% have **some college attended**, 19% have a **bachelor’s degree**, 14% have an **associates degree** and 8% **possess a post graduate degree** of a masters or doctorate.
Understanding these demographics and several others can be useful to both existing and new businesses while assisting with better knowledge of customer base within the City of Tehachapi trade area.

Using this evidence-based approach, business owners and developers can target specific areas of the population for business recruitment and assist in retention efforts by better positioning goods and services available to the customers they serve.

The commercial real estate and development markets continue to be impacted by national economic conditions, in a secondary market like the City of Tehachapi, those conditions can lead to a more challenging retail and restaurant recruitment effort as national brands scale back due to conditions.

Recently at a Greater Tehachapi Economic Development Council meeting, the City of Tehachapi addressed this subject with a few recent interactions with developers and the reality of the conditions to recruit new business into the community.

With the most recent quarter-point interest rate increase by the Federal Reserve, the 10 th rate hike in the last 14 months, the benchmark rate now sits between 5 and 5.25%, up from 0% in March of 2022 and now the highest interest rate in 16 years.
Increased rates to this level and volatile supply and labor conditions have increased the price to not only get a loan from a bank, but physically build a project.
Additionally, bank failures that once served venture capitalists and investors such as Silicon Valley Bank and First Republic Bank are causing additional funding challenges for commercial developers.
Recently, Berkshire-Hathaway’s Charlie Munger told The Financial Times he worried about “bad loans” of troubled shopping malls and office buildings.

On May 8 th, CoStar News reported that the loan tied to WeWork’s San Francisco office has gone into default, a trend that some expect to continue and have ramifications throughout the banking industry.

In a secondary market like Tehachapi, most national expansions are reserved for more stable economic times as our market size sometimes requires more time to recoup the investment costs of either corporate or franchise-owned locations.

A few years ago, a similar conversation with the national chicken chain Raising Cane’s suggested that since the company invests more money than many other chains on their site development, that a market like Tehachapi would take longer than the company was comfortable with to recoup that investment and see returns.
Historically, economic recessions usually mean higher sales for quick serve and fast-food restaurants, however, food prices have impacted even the historically “cheap” menus.

This was seen in the recent earnings report from McDonald’s who posted positive first quarter earnings, but their CEO Chris Kempczinski went on record claiming the company was receiving “pushback” for higher prices and customers are buying fewer items than before as items per transaction have fallen.
For the City of Tehachapi, the approach to recruitment will continue to be based on data-driven solutions to match tenants with the most successful sites available.
This will also mean a relative slowdown in new business development that requires significant investment.
At the upcoming ICSC conference in Las Vegas, the approach will continue to be relationship-driven as many of these companies take several years to develop in our community.

While they may not be developing in the next 12-24 months, these opportunities to meet, educate and promote the City of Tehachapi has historically paid off with retail investment when the economy improves.

These unstable commercial real estate conditions do provide opportunities as well, as retail vacancies become available, reuse of these sites to bring in new business for a smaller investment than building new becomes a possibility for some if the location fits the proforma.
Additionally, small businesses can benefit as well with lower rents or other expansion; if funding sources are not too challenging as previously discussed.
Fortunately, in the City of Tehachapi, small business continues to thrive.

While some are dealing with a slow down due to cost increases and consumers spending a little less, new and expanded businesses have come to find a home in the city, others have also relocated as opportunities closer to their industry audience or target customers have come available.
As with anything in economic development, this dynamic process continues to adapt to market conditions to provide the best possible service to the community.

As Tehachapi enters the final quarter of 2022, some recent data sheds light on the availability of retail properties both in the City of Tehachapi and southeastern Kern County.

Recent reports from CoStar, the City’s commercial real estate service shows the area with a 3.3% vacancy rate amongst commercial retail properties in this submarket which includes the City of Tehachapi, the Greater Tehachapi Area, Mojave, Rosamond, Arvin and a portion of unincorporated Bakersfield.
The Capital Hills area in the City of Tehachapi which sits north of Highway 58 is not included in this submarket and therefore the recent construction of a hotel and shopping center are not captured.

The 3.3% vacancy rate is under the national five-year average while retail rents have risen 3.8% over the last 12 months with the average price of $262 s.f. sitting above the region’s average pricing as well.
With less space and a more captive audience in smaller communities that trend is not unexpected when compared to a larger retail metropolitan area.
The historical vacancy rate sits around 4.4% on average with CoStar projections showing just a slight increase to from 3.3% to 3.4% for the next 12 months in the submarket.

Two of the most active three-star rated buildings (CoStar rankings) are in the City of Tehachapi with four leases signed over the last 12 months taking a total of 8,600 s.f. of retail space off the market.
Two of the three highest rated and highest priced-submarket properties have been sold in the City of Tehachapi in the last 12 months.
Commercial real estate investment continues in the City of Tehachapi as investors have spent millions in the last few months on some marquee properties in transactions with long-term stable tenants.
As part of a new initiative, the City of Tehachapi has partnered with CoStar to access real-time commercial real estate data to assist in economic development efforts.
This software is a powerful tool that generates reports on active sales, sales histories, comparable properties, lease rates, vacancies, owner information and much more.

In a secondary market like Tehachapi, this data was previously difficult to acquire, now it is a useful tool to complement the use of Placer A.I. for location data used to record visits to commercial properties and special events.
This latest tool has already shown several important numbers that show the City of Tehachapi as a magnet for investment.

When commercial properties are built, they oftentimes have a shelf life, however, the City of Tehachapi has been able to help increase both the viability and the value of many properties thanks in part to a robust regional economy, diverse shopping base, proper planning and public/private projects that have helped raise values of shopping centers and encouraged more investment.
Earlier this year, the Walgreens on Tehachapi Boulevard which was constructed in 2003 sold for $6.4 million to an investment company.
Walgreens has a strong history in Tehachapi and has another 11 years remaining on the lease of the 14,560 s.f. retail corner.
The building first sold in 2014 for $5.4 million.
Market-rent-per area shows this property has increased in value over four percent in the last 12 months.
Most recently, the Albertson’s building---another prime commercial property with a stable grocery tenant since 1994, sold for $22.25 million to another real estate investment firm.
This property had previously sold in 2020 for $14 million and fetched a large price tag due to the stability of the tenant and the production of the grocery store.
Additionally, the Market-rent-per area report from CoStar also shows a four percent increase in property value over the last 12 months for this building.
These two commercial sales represent nearly $30 million in investment in the Tehachapi market in the last six months alone.
It should be noted that the sales were due in part to the stability of the tenants and that the current tenants will remain in operation.

CoStar also classifies the majority of the City of Tehachapi as a Southeast Kern County submarket of Bakersfield, with one of the lowest vacancy rates in the county at just 3.1% with projections over the next six months showing a small .04% change.

CoStar also describes the rent rates in this submarket as higher because retail tenants are willing to pay a premium to reside in the SE Kern County submarket which commands a materially higher price than the metro area.
Rents in the submarket average $23.00 s.f./triple net, compared to $18.60 s.f./triple net in the Bakersfield metro.
This was linked to the submarket’s amount of new retail space constructed in the last decade compared to that of Bakersfield metro.

These data tools from CoStar and others will allow the economic development efforts in the City of Tehachapi to leverage real time pricing data for new and existing retail space, assist local agents and brokers with leasing efforts and continue to showcase the successful retail market that exists in the City of Tehachapi for businesses of all size looking to invest and move their services to our city.
The economic impact of special events in the City of Tehachapi is an important economic driver for both locals and tourists alike.
There is the benefit of these events, whether it is hotel stays for larger events or additional revenue for small and large businesses while people visit Tehachapi and Downtown specifically.

There is also the impact brought on by the event itself, this includes the time by City Public Works, Police and administrative staff to ensure the event is safe, efficient and secure for all those participating.

Oftentimes much of these expenses are absorbed by City departments although the economic return to the city does not cover the costs, the positivity brought on by these events pays dividends in the future.
The City of Tehachapi is one of the only small communities in Kern County that continues to host special events, a testament to the desirability of our community.

Summertime brings a host of events and using our data from Placer A.I., the City of Tehachapi can evaluate the attendance of these events to work with event organizers to ensure future planning needs are met as events grow and expand.
This is done to ensure enough services such as restrooms, police officers, sanitation and road closures are provided.

The value of these events can be found in the tourism created, for example the Mountain Festival drew enough visitors from areas as far north as Fresno to as far south as Irvine along with a tremendous visitation from nearby communities such as Bakersfield and the Antelope Valley.
These visitors often become customers of other local businesses, restaurants and purchase hotel rooms and fuel before leaving our community.
These visit trends are similar with many events in the City of Tehachapi.
The City of Tehachapi continues to seek ways to support special events that choose to operate in the city while balancing responsibilities between event organizers and City staff.
With that sort of balance and partnership, the economic impact and benefit to our local businesses can far outweigh the fiscal and physical impact on City staff and finances.
We look forward to another summer of events in 2023.

As communities become a more attractive place to do business, there are certain unseen circumstances that make conducting ongoing recruitment efforts a little more challenging than many think.
For example, the complex world of commercial real estate leases, especially with those that have broader business implications, can impact even small communities such as the City of Tehachapi.
When a business closes naturally the assumption is that a vacant retail suite is just that, vacant and in turn, available for lease.

However, in many cases, including a couple in Tehachapi, property owners—and any economic development recruiters, must pause their efforts to find new tenants until the lease term expires as to not interfere with the closing organizations’ business efforts.
There are a few examples of that currently in our community, and while residents understandably ask the “why don’t they…” question about a retail vacancy, it helps to understand the entire picture.
One of the most-glaring cases of this is the former Kmart building on Tehachapi Boulevard.
The business closed in 2019 in line with the bankruptcy filings of the company and the mass-shuttering of stores nationwide.
However, that building remains under lease from the holdings company associated with the former Kmart corporation.
As is the case with any active lease, any recruitment efforts for new tenants or redevelopment is prohibited as the lease remains active although the business is closed.
Oftentimes a first right of refusal to renew those leases is available as well.
Recently the Dollar Tree corporation purchased the Family Dollar stores leading to a downsizing of stores across the country including the Family Dollar location in the City of Tehachapi.
Since Tehachapi had both brands, the Family Dollar location on Tucker Road was shuttered as the company reorganizes their assets.
This former store too is still under an active lease for the 6,000 square-foot retail suite and is not available for lease until the current lease expires.
The active lease also restricts recruiting potential replacement tenants.

This creates a unique situation for the City of Tehachapi as our economic profile is one that is attractive to more retailers, however with vacant space that is technically not available for lease, this can have a negative impact on the market.

Site selectors see these locations as potential sites for redevelopment, and since tenant improvements tend to be much cheaper than building a new project, especially given the costs of goods and services along with construction supply issues recently, situations such as this sometimes delay retail development and potential new businesses elect to wait longer to open in a market like Tehachapi.

While facilities like the former Kmart building continue to be on the wish list for redevelopment by new retail tenants, it will remain vacant until at which time an active lease is no longer present.

As with the case of any business in the City of Tehachapi, the code enforcement division through the Tehachapi Police Department continues to ensure properties do not fall into visual disrepair or become a chronic nuisance or magnet for criminal activity.

As part of the ongoing analysis associated with businesses in the City of Tehachapi and the residents that they serve in this community and their surrounding neighbors, another recent study shows an even larger footprint that previously expected.
Using Placer a.i. and STI Popstats, an analysis of location data for the 2021 calendar year shows a true trade area (people who shop here regularly) of over 215,000 residents.

The dataset sets a 50-mile radius around the city, however it only accounts for those trips into Tehachapi that account for 70% or more of the traffic, focusing on repeat-shoppers and not a one-stop traveler.

With the increased retail offerings in Tehachapi, those communities in the trade area include all of those in the 93561 Tehachapi zip code as well as California City, Mojave and portions of Rosamond and Bakersfield.
This data significantly increases the number of shoppers in both large retail centers along with the residual benefits to surrounding restaurants, fuel stations and specialty stores.

In capturing a demographic profile of the most-frequent-visitors, the 37,000 living within a 15-mile radius of the City of Tehachapi, the average age is 42 years old, the average household income is $88,000 per year while 20% of households average between $100,000 and $150,000 per year.

The diversity of employment sectors continues with retail trade, healthcare, education and public administration (including law enforcement, corrections and fire) accounting for 48% of the jobs for residents.

While both sets of data tell a story about who is living in the area and those that are coming to shop, dine and spend money in the city, the economic power of both continues to increase making the City of Tehachapi an attractive destination for investors and business owners.

**Strengths**: Diversity within the Tehachapi economy continues to be our most beneficial strength.
It assists in limiting the impact felt to the community due to any one job sector in uncertain economic times and provides for a myriad of business opportunities when expansion is in the cards.

Tehachapi is strategically located near several successful industries making our city a key supporter of several expanding job opportunities including renewable energy, space exploration, aerospace and mining in East Kern, and many professional, legal, and business services in the southern San Joaquin Valley.
A robust construction climate as well has bolstered that industry for both public and private projects.

Kern County leads the state in renewable energy production and development of new energy technologies, Tehachapi residents and companies benefit from the economic impact of these projects and will continue as those markets expand.
**Weaknesses**: With all these expanding sectors, especially in East Kern, new employees need housing.
Tehachapi is the top choice for many of these companies when their employees are new to the area.

After several slow years, housing production is starting to ramp up in the City of Tehachapi, but a lack of inventory has increased prices dramatically both in the City and in the Greater Tehachapi Area.
Prices that are too high because of lack of inventory create unaffordability for both the next generation of locals and potential new employees for growing businesses.

There are currently 138 homes of various price points in four tracts under construction in the city, while the Tehachapi Planning Commission recently approved the precise development plan for the 250-unit The Address at Tehachapi project.
That approval clears the way for construction to begin within the next 12 months.
Other previously approved developments continue to work towards their construction process.
These new units should settle the housing market, opening availability for professionals and benefitting business expansion so employees can afford reasonably priced homes.
**Opportunities:** There are several areas locally in the retail sector that have plenty of room for growth given the lack of supply but a steady demand for those goods.

According to STI Market Outlook, there is over $2 million in unmet demand in the City of Tehachapi trade area in each of the following categories: home furnishings, specialty food stores, health and personal care, clothing and shoe stores, limited service and special food service restaurants.
These areas continue to be targets of economic development and real estate broker efforts in 2022.
This year will also continue the shift of how people work, and Tehachapi is prepared to meet that shift.

While many used the pandemic as a reason to start a new business or become self-employed, 2022 is the year that the resources they need to both be successful and grow their businesses become available.
Places like the Village Collective will be complete downtown offering new boutique office space and a shared co-working environment.
Coupled with the completion of the Race Communications fiber optic project throughout the city, internet demand will be met with this high bandwidth technology.

In addition, several of the aforementioned housing projects under construction are taking the way many live and work into consideration and offering housing models with dedicated separate spaces for potential home offices.
There were 167 new business licenses filed in the City of Tehachapi in 2021, an indication of the new entrepreneurial spirit and the City is prepared to offer support and tools for success in 2022.
**Threats:** The City of Tehachapi can benefit from being located in the State of California and can also be threatened by that reality as well.
Sacramento money grabs and unfunded mandates from the State Legislature weaken the ability for both residents, businesses and even City government to operate in an efficient manner.
Millions of local dollars have been kept by Sacramento in recent years, impacting local services and the ability to make our economy and community even stronger.

Restrictions of how businesses operate, new mandates and laws continue to drive the cost of doing business up, leading to higher prices and other trickle-down impacts due to Sacramento’s one-size-fits-all approach.
Finding ways to establish more local control of funding will be critical to address this threat moving forward.
Inflation is also a contributing factor to higher prices and a threat to consider in 2022 for the local economy.
The consumer price index rose 7% in December, the fastest pace since 1982.
Excluding food and energy, the core CPI was up 5.5% over last year, the biggest increase since February 1991.
With a large commuting population, higher prices at the pumps will contribute to an adjustment in spending elsewhere.
While 2022 will mark the two-year anniversary of COVID-19, the area is still dealing with the fallout.

With some exceptions, life has returned to normal in Tehachapi, but the economic impact remains, ever shifting and conflicting guidance from the CDC, the California Department of Public Health and Cal OSHA make it difficult to keep businesses efficiently staffed.

Decisions will have to be made in 2022 to figure out how to start living with these less-potent variants of COVID-19, less the impact to the workforce start causing disruptions to the economy not seen since the initial COVID-prompted shutdowns of 2020.

Maintaining vital infrastructure continues to be a facet of economic development in the City of Tehachapi and a slough of recent projects are once again proving that priority with action.
The City of Tehachapi recently re-paved three local roadways as part of a series of maintenance projects.
One roadway, Green Street, received new asphalt from Tehachapi Boulevard north to the Tehachapi Municipal Airport gate, as well as from ‘F’ Street south past ‘D’ Street.

With those portions joining the recently slurry-sealed section of Green between Tehachapi Boulevard and ‘F’ Street, the road that serves many local businesses, special events and the airport has received a complete makeover in the last six months.

In addition, Davis Street from Tehachapi Boulevard to E Street received much-needed pavement while Snyder Avenue, a major route for Tehachapi schools and connector from Valley Boulevard to Tehachapi Boulevard was also paved, weaving together a pair of projects, the first of which included new curbs, gutters and sidewalks and the new pavement for a new safer path of travel for both pedestrians and vehicles alike.
Fog sealant application and striping will mark the finishing touches on these projects.
In addition, the recently-completed Rail Corridor Enhancement and Pedestrian Safety Project was recognized as “Transportation Project of the Year” by the American Society of Civil Engineers.
The Rail Corridor Pedestrian Safety & Enhancement Project included sidewalks and fencing along H Street on the North side of the train tracks between Mill Street and Hayes Street.
Sidewalks and crossings on the East and West sides of Green Street, Hayes Street and Dennison Road.
The crossings provided a much safer path of travel for pedestrians, cyclists, and those in wheelchairs.
It also meant the installation of medians at the crossings to prevent vehicles from driving around railroad gates and potentially into the path of crossing trains.
The Tehachapi Rail Corridor Pedestrian Safety & Enhancement Project had a total project cost of $2.1 million dollars, and the construction was completed in approximately 12 months.
The project was funded by the Active Transportation Project grant.
The rail corridor project served an important role in extending the ability for visitors and shoppers to access ‘H’ Street, a natural extension of Downtown.
The area has attracted investments from microbreweries and small retail shops in the last few years with more small business investments under construction.

Not only providing opportunities for investment, but also delivering the ability for those investments to thrive with maintenance of infrastructure, police protection and continued support of businesses of all sizes continue to push the City of Tehachapi as a great place for success.

Through a partnership with Placer AI, the City of Tehachapi has been able to access the economic recovery dashboard that is showing a 115% recovery of the tourism industry in Tehachapi following the COVID-19 related shutdowns.
This data, compared to the same time periods in 2019, shows that both domestic (>51 to 150 miles) and national tourism (<150 miles) to Tehachapi has recovered at 115% of the levels show in 2019.
This is based on foot traffic to the tourist attractions in the City and Greater Tehachapi area.
The most recent numbers, recorded in June 2021, show an estimated 128,500 visitors to Tehachapi compared to 115,000 in June of 2019.
The weekly numbers do show nearly 20,000 additional visitors during the July 4 th weekend than the 2019 festivities with national tourism increasing 150%.
An encouraging sign is the hotel occupancy with 108% recovery since the Summer of 2019.
This falls in line with the increase in tourists from distances greater than 150 miles.

Other news related to recovery shows the retail industry has recovered at over 118% compared to the same time in 2019, most of that credited to the expanded trade area of Tehachapi with increased traffic from surrounding communities.

Grocery stores are still below pre-pandemic levels at 76%, but the trend of panic buying impacted the foot traffic to stores as residents shopped for more items on one trip rather than visit a grocery store on a weekly basis.
The local restaurant industry, heavily impacted by COVID-19 shut downs has recovered at 93% compared to 2019.
Home improvement stores and superstores have recovered well above 100%.
With a variety of events scheduled and the presence of additional tourism-related activities in the Tehachapi area, this recovery should continue through the summer and autumn months.

Aside from the empirical data one notices with fewer parking stalls full and fewer cars on the road, what was impact of COVID-19 on the daily driving habits in Kern County?
Streetlight Data recently released a county-by-county interactive tool that showcases the ability to see adjusted vehicle miles traveled (VMT) from the start of the pandemic to current day.
This data and algorithm are updated every two days.
While the data is not broken down specifically by city, the Kern County data paints a consistent picture with the economy, COVID-19 response and who is driving less as a result.
For example, the biggest drop was immediate, with Kern County driving 31% less on April 1 st, just after lockdown measures, stay-at-home orders and many businesses were shuttered.
This represents a reduction from over 26 million miles driven as of March 1 st, to 17.3 million miles on April 1 st.

Running the numbers for just the first of every month shows a 14% reduction in May, a 17% reduction in June, a 4% reduction in July (after things had opened up slightly before being rolled back again), a 4% reduction from baseline in August and a 9% reduction as of the most recent data in September.
This data shows Kern County is still driving less than the time prior to COVID-19 but has slowly been increasing VMT over the last several months.
This data is important to economic development, especially in communities like Tehachapi where the traveling public is vital to the local economy along with the major trade corridor of Highway 58.

Also, new additions like restaurants, retail and other business ventures rely on either local workforce during the day or focus on commuting traffic early in the morning or in the evening for purchases.
You can access the tool here https://www.streetlightdata.com/VMT-monitor-by-county/#methodology and see how Tehachapi and Kern County are stacking up with the rest of the country.

The New Normal: When Business Reopens, What Will That Look Like?

Our direction continues to be vague about when business will “get back to normal,” but rest assured the City of Tehachapi staff has dedicated countless hours to gathering as much data as possible to help local business prepare for when whatever new version of “normal” we receive when the economy reopens.
The restaurant industry has been one of the hardest hit economically both locally and nationally.

Estimates from Hathaway Consumer Insights claims that in a recent study 26% of consumers claim they won’t return to eating in restaurants after COVID-19 and they aren’t planning on ordering out during the current state of affairs.
While some will stray from this assertion, this could lead to increased competition in the industry.
All statistics/studies are open to interpretation.
This particular study was conducted in New York City, where the outbreak of COVID-19 was far worse than what we’ve seen in Kern County and Tehachapi specifically.
Based on the local response and desire to support local restaurants, takeout orders have been steady and the desire to return to their favorite eateries is present.
Will 26% not eat out during or after COVID-19?
Unlikely the number will be that high locally but in a community with a large number of elderly and vulnerable population some decline in available customers is to be expected.
What does that mean for a restaurant owner?

For starters, much of the new business practices being adopted such as online ordering, strong social media presence, curbside pickup, apps and delivery will continue to be a relevant part of the “new normal” upon reopening in full capacity.

In some of our data collecting its been noted that restaurants such as Wingstop and Buffalo Wild Wings are experiencing an increase in business due to their previous investment in technology and curbside pickup.
Others are reporting that delivery and curbside pickups are helping ease the strain, but not completely replacing lost revenue during the shutdown.
What will the new normal look like?
It’s tough to say.

Some basic principles mentioned by Governor Gavin Newsom two weeks ago include disposable paper menus for restaurants, reduced capacity and fewer tables as well as a potential for temperature checks at the door (although these normally require a trained medical professional in every other case so don’t put too much worry into that).
*   Continue building online, telephone, delivery and curbside pickup options.

*   Invest in technology which includes a website, a simple online ordering platform and if possible an app to help your business be more mobile-friendly to capture the majority of the online activity.

*   Find creative ways to replace, clean or bring awareness to commonly-touched spaces in your business such as doorknobs, light switches, etc. Some companies are putting bright stickers next to them which will remind employees to either wash hands or sanitize after touching them.
Studies are currently underway in countries that are attempting their recovery from coronavirus-shutdowns.
Early data shows a 16% increase in only ordering in China since they reopened their economy, other data will be forthcoming as additional states in the U.S. open their doors as well.
Here’s more from Inc.com about preparing for reopening your business for a post COVID-19 economy.
The National Restaurant Association recently released some draft guidelines for opening dining rooms across America.
Click the link and download the resource guide filled with best practices, many which can be planned now so you’re prepared for in-person dining as soon as it is allowable.
We will continue to gather best practices, information and communicate them as part of our economic development efforts as we focus on recovery.

The City of Tehachapi held a special City Council meeting on Wednesday, March 18, 2020 on the steps of City Hall where at the suggestion of the Economic Development Department, authorized a temporary program to defer utility payments for small businesses in the City of Tehachapi.

According to the SBA, the agency will work with state governors to provide targeted, low-interest disaster recovery loads to small businesses that have severely been impacted by the situation.

*   Loans are 30 year loans.

*   SBA’s Office of Disaster Assistance will coordinate with the state’s or territory’s Governor to submit the request for Economic Injury Disaster Loan assistance.

*   SBA offers loans with long-term repayments in order to keep payments affordable, up to a maximum of 30 years.
Terms are determined on a case-by-case basis, based upon each borrower’s ability to repay.
